p: This book is set at Halcyon AI in Denver. Ninety or so engineers work there, plus a group in Kraków, Poland, eight hours ahead.
Halcyon sells Lumen, which tells hospitals when their patients are likely to go home, so some of its code sits close to patient data.
Priya Shah runs the platform Lumen sits on, a job she inherited six months ago.
Her family is close by: her father, Raj, who spent his working life at a lathe and still lives in Aurora, and his sister Asha, a retired ER nurse who lives four streets over.
The people you'll hear from first.
Asha Shah. Priya's aunt. She'll answer a question with a question.
Elena Vasquez. Halcyon's founder and boss. She writes her emails early.
Joyce Cho. The CTO. She answers to Elena.
Anders Lindqvist. Built Halcyon's platform, and taught Priya most of what she knows about it.
Devin Marsh. Engineer. Fast at everything, and already letting Copilot write whole functions.
Ken Ito. Runs security and privacy. Quiet, and very hard to rush.
The email arrived at 6:12 on a Monday morning, which meant Elena had written it on the treadmill.

An email from Elena Vasquez. Subject: Copilot, this quarter. Team, Every engineer at Halcyon will be using GitHub Copilot by the end of the quarter. Our competitors already are. Priya Shah will lead the rollout and has my full support. Joyce is the sponsor. Please give Priya whatever she needs. Elena

Priya Shah read it on her phone in the parking garage, still in the car, the engine off and the radio still talking about the Broncos. She read it a second time to make sure her name was actually in it. It was. It was in the same sentence as "full support," which at Halcyon could mean anything from a real budget to a blessing and a deadline.

Six months ago she'd been a data engineer who kept quiet in meetings. Then Anders Lindqvist took another job, and somebody had to own the platform, and the somebody turned out to be her. Then she moved Lumen, the discharge forecasting product Halcyon sold to hospitals, onto the new platform. It was her first project with her name at the top of the plan, and it shipped on time because she'd been too scared to let it slip. Now this. A rollout to ninety engineers, most of them older than her, several of them people who had trained her. Every team she'd led so far had wanted her there. These people hadn't.

Her phone buzzed before she got to the elevator. Anders, who was back at Halcyon on a six month contract, which still felt strange. congrats on the robot job. I'll trust it when it can explain my own Terraform to me.

She typed three replies and deleted all of them. Then she texted her aunt Asha five words before she'd decided to: I got the Copilot thing. Asha Shah had been an ER nurse for thirty years, first in Greeley and then in Denver, most of them on nights and most of those as charge nurse, and somewhere along the way she'd become the person Priya called before she panicked. The phone rang before Priya reached her desk.
Saw it, Asha said. Before you do anything, what do you actually know about how people there use Copilot today?
Asha let that sit a second. That's the right starting point. I'll send you something by lunch.

At 11:50 her phone buzzed with five photos of index cards covered in purple felt tip. Asha used to hand a stack like it to every new nurse on her shift. Across the top card she'd written: Shift notes for a new kind of copilot. Read before you start.
Asha's Shift Notes: what you're actually rolling out.
Asha's first card was underlined twice. Before you hook a patient up to a new machine, know exactly which machine it is.

Under each card Priya wrote what the GitHub docs said. GitHub Copilot comes in individual plans and organization plans. The individual plans are Copilot Free, Copilot Student, Copilot Pro, Copilot Pro+, and Copilot Max. Free is for trying it out, with limits, including a cap on inline suggestions each month. Student is free for verified students. Pro, Pro+, and Max add more models and larger usage allowances for one person, who pays for it and manages it.

The organization plans are Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise. Business is for organizations and adds the thing a rollout needs most: centralized management and policy control over the people the organization gives a seat to. Enterprise includes everything in Business plus enterprise grade capabilities and a larger usage allowance, and it's for companies on GitHub Enterprise Cloud. Copilot doesn't run on GitHub Enterprise Server itself. A company on Server can get Copilot through an enterprise account on GitHub Enterprise Cloud instead. Today GitHub measures usage in AI credits, with a monthly allowance by plan. Older study material and some exam questions may still say "premium requests." Learn the stable idea: plans include a usage allowance, and heavier features and models use more of it.

How the exam asks it. When a question asks which plan lets an organization set policies for its members, the answer is Business or Enterprise. When it mentions GitHub Enterprise Cloud and enterprise grade features, lean Enterprise. An individual plan never gives the company control.

Copilot shows up in several places, and the exam expects you to know which is which. In the editor you get inline suggestions as you type, Copilot Chat in a side panel, and agent mode, where Copilot makes multi file edits and proposes terminal commands while you watch and approve. In the terminal there's GitHub Copilot CLI. On GitHub.com you get chat, pull request summaries, Copilot code review, and the coding agent you can assign an issue to.

The editor support comes from extensions. GitHub documents setup for Visual Studio Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs, Vim and Neovim, Xcode, and Eclipse. GitHub.com is not an IDE, and there's no GitHub.com extension to install. To turn Copilot on in an editor, you install the extension and sign in with the GitHub account that holds the Copilot seat. Signed in with the wrong account, a developer sees nothing, and it looks like Copilot is broken.

Priya added a note for the skeptics, since Anders would ask first. The quiet case for Copilot in the editor is less context switching. Half the team kept the wiki open in a browser all day, and every trip out there cost them the line they'd been holding in their head. With Chat in the side panel, you can select a block nobody remembers writing and ask Copilot to explain the code, right in the file. It works when you learn a new language too. Priya's first month on Terraform, she didn't know what a provider block was. She'd have asked what a line did, then asked for a smaller example. But learning faster isn't trusting faster. An explanation is a lead. Check it against the code, or run terraform plan and see if the answer holds up.
How the exam asks it. Expect a list of environments with one that doesn't belong. GitHub.com is the usual trap: Copilot works there, but it isn't an IDE extension.
Turning it on for an organization.

An organization owner manages Copilot from the organization's Settings, under Copilot. The Access page is where seats are granted, either to all members, which covers current and future members, or to selected teams and members. Billing starts when a seat is granted, not when someone first uses it. Seats can also be managed through the REST API, which is how larger companies automate it.

The Policies page controls which features are available and the privacy related settings, and the Models page controls access to models beyond the basic ones. Watch one of those features. On Business and Enterprise seats, next edit suggestions in VS Code stay off until the organization or enterprise enables the Editor preview features policy, so a developer can turn the setting on and still see nothing. If the organization belongs to an enterprise, enterprise policies win. When an enterprise owner sets a policy, the organization can't override it. The audit log records Copilot plan and policy changes and seats being added or removed. It does not include the prompts people send to Copilot in their editors. Events are kept for 180 days, so a company that needs longer evidence exports the log on a schedule, or streams it if it's on GitHub Enterprise Cloud.
How the exam asks it. Know who wins: enterprise policy over organization policy. Know what the audit log shows: settings, policy changes, and seat changes, not prompts or suggestions.

Here Asha had drawn a box with a line running outside it. Organization policies apply to the seats the organization grants. Content exclusions, which stop Copilot from using chosen files or repositories as context, are a Business and Enterprise feature, and an organization owner sets them for the people who have a seat through that organization. A developer using a personal Pro plan on company code is outside that box. The company can't apply its policies to that plan, can't see it in its audit log, and can't promise an auditor what it did.
How the exam asks it. If a scenario says some developers use personal plans and the company wants consistent policies or exclusions, the answer moves them onto organization seats.
The last card was short. A monitor can be confidently wrong. Check the patient, not the screen.

Generative AI predicts likely output from patterns. That means it can produce code that looks right and isn't, use outdated or insecure patterns, invent an API that doesn't exist, reflect bias in its training data, or produce code that matches public code with a license attached. The mitigations are ordinary engineering discipline: a human reviews it, tests prove it, and the person who accepts a suggestion owns it exactly as if they'd typed it.

The model behind Copilot is a large language model, or LLM: software trained on a huge amount of text and code to predict what comes next. Three of its limits come up again and again. The first is the context window. A model can only hold so much at once. Ninety engineers' worth of code won't fit, and whatever's left out doesn't exist for it. The second is the training cutoff. The model learned from data up to a date, so a library released after that may be missing or described the old way. The third is that the output is nondeterministic. Ask the same thing twice and you can get two different answers, so one good run proves nothing. None of these are filter failures. The filters catch harmful output, and if someone's switched on blocking, they drop code that matches public code. They can't make a wrong answer right. And confidence is just how the model writes. It isn't a sign that the answer is true.

Under the last card Priya wrote down how it actually works. When you ask Copilot for something, it builds a prompt from what you typed plus context from your editor, like the file you're in, the code near your cursor, and other open files. That prompt goes to the Copilot service, passes through filters, and the response is filtered again before it reaches you.

Priya tested it at her own desk. With only a new test file open, the inline suggestions were generic. She opened the module under test in a second tab, typed the same first line, and this time the suggestion used the module's real function names. Inline, Copilot reads mostly the code around the cursor, the file's name and language, and the other open tabs. Chat starts from the file you're looking at and anything you've selected, and you can pull in more with file references, like #file in VS Code. Agent mode goes hunting through the project for relevant context by itself. Two things stay out. A closed file nobody mentioned usually isn't in an inline prompt, even if it's right there in the repo. And where content exclusions are supported, an excluded file stays out even while it's open. Ken would want that last one written in pen.
At the bottom of the last card Asha had written one more line. Better context in, better answers out. Everything out still gets checked.
How the exam asks it. Responsible use answers almost always include human review and testing. "Trust it because it's usually right" is the wrong answer every time.

At nine that morning, before the cards came, Priya already had a blank document titled "Copilot rollout" and eleven Slack messages asking when people would "get it." Joyce Cho stopped by with coffee and the look of a sponsor who would rather not be asked hard questions.
Elena wants a plan by Friday. What do you need? Priya didn't know yet. That was the problem.
A. Survey the engineers on who already uses Copilot, on what plan.
B. Buy Business seats today for all ninety engineers on the org account.
C. Book a demo with GitHub sales this week and decide the plan from it.
D. Ask Anders, the engineer people listen to, which plan Halcyon should buy.

The survey takes two days and fifty seven people answer. Thirty one are already using Copilot. Most are on personal plans they expense. They use five different editors. Two people are pasting code into a chatbot in a browser tab. None of this was on any diagram.

That's the one I'd sign. Assess before you act. You can't pick a plan, set policies, or plan training until you know what's already happening. The current state is always messier than the org chart says.

The survey had a free text box, and people used it. One answer said: "I use Neovim, so I assume I'm out." Another said: "Can we install the GitHub.com extension so it works in the browser?" A third said Xcode, from the one engineer who still maintained the old iPad app.
Priya needed to answer before the questions turned into folklore.
Engineers ask about Neovim, Xcode and a GitHub.com extension. What should Priya tell them?
A. Say Neovim and Xcode have Copilot extensions and GitHub.com has it built in.
B. Move everyone onto VS Code, Neovim and Xcode users included, for the rollout.
C. Point the Neovim and Xcode users to Copilot Chat on GitHub.com instead.
D. Say Neovim is supported and a GitHub.com extension is coming, and check on Xcode.

She posts the supported list from GitHub's docs in the channel: VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs, Vim and Neovim, Xcode, Eclipse. And a line underneath: GitHub.com isn't an IDE, so there's nothing to install there. The Neovim engineer replies with a single thumbs up, which from him is a parade.
That's how I'd chart it. Know the supported editors. Neovim and Xcode both have Copilot support. GitHub.com isn't an IDE extension at all. Copilot is part of the site itself.

Wednesday Priya sat down with the account details. Halcyon's code lived in a GitHub organization on the Team plan. Nobody had ever moved it to GitHub Enterprise Cloud. Anders had said Enterprise. Devin had said, in the survey, "Pro is ten bucks, just expense it for everybody."
What she needed, more than anything, was a way to set rules once and have them apply to everyone.
Anders says Enterprise, and Devin says expense Pro for everybody. Which Copilot plan fits?
A. Whatever plan each team lead picks, matched to that team's work.
B. Copilot Business now, revisited if Halcyon moves to Enterprise Cloud.
C. Copilot Pro for each engineer, expensed the way most already do it.
D. Copilot Enterprise for every engineer now, the plan Anders recommended.

She picks Copilot Business, on the organization Halcyon already has, and Joyce signs off in ten minutes. Priya writes down the condition that would change the answer: if Halcyon ever moves to GitHub Enterprise Cloud, look at Enterprise again. It goes in the plan as a dated decision, not a vague maybe.

That's what I'd want on my shift. Business gives an organization central seat management and policy control, which is the core need. Enterprise is for organizations on GitHub Enterprise Cloud that want its enterprise grade capabilities. Pick what fits today and write down what would change it.
Thirty one engineers already used Copilot. Twenty six of them did it on personal Pro plans, on company code, expensed or paid out of pocket.
Devin was one of them, and he wasn't shy about it. Mine works fine. I've got my settings how I like them. Just let us keep what we have and give seats to everybody else.
A few people in the channel added a plus one. Priya felt the old pull to keep the peace.
Devin wants the people on personal Pro plans to keep them. What should Priya do?
A. Let personal plan users keep them and give org seats only to the rest.
B. Block personal plan accounts from company repos until each one is canceled.
C. Require org seats at work and let people keep personal plans for home.
D. Move everyone onto org seats and sit with anyone who needs help switching.

She writes a short note: one plan, one set of rules, one audit trail, and why that matters for code that touches patient workflows. She offers to sit with anyone moving over. Devin grumbles, then asks her to help him find where his editor settings live. They do it in ten minutes.

That's the one I'd sign. Consistency is the point of an organization plan. Explain the reason, not just the rule, and make the switch easy. People accept a change when they understand it and someone helps them through it.
Thursday's kickoff had sixty people on the call and Anders in the front row of the conference room, arms folded.
Devin got there first. Honestly the main thing is speed. It writes it, I ship it. Why would I reread code the machine already wrote?
Anders didn't look up. And that's why I'll be on call.
Sixty people waited to see what the new rollout lead would say.
Devin says he ships Copilot's code without rereading it. How should Priya respond?
A. Limit Copilot to tests plus docs until it earns the team's trust.
B. Let Anders and Devin argue it out on the call for the whole team to hear.
C. Agree speed matters and count on the CI pipeline to catch what slips.
D. Set the rule that whoever accepts a suggestion owns it like anything they typed.

She puts it on the shared screen in one line: you own what you accept. Then she asks Anders what he'd look for in a review of Copilot code. He's surprised to be asked. His list is good, and it goes in the guide.

That's how I'd chart it. Responsible use starts with accountability. Copilot helps, and you still own the result. Treat its output like code from a new teammate: read it, understand it, and test it before it ships.
Joyce caught her after the kickoff. Can we just turn it on for everyone Friday? Elena would love to see the number go to ninety.
Priya knew what the Access page offered. One button covered all members, current and future. The other let her pick teams.
Joyce wants Copilot turned on for everyone Friday. How should Priya assign seats?
A. Wait until next quarter and turn it on for every member at once.
B. Grant seats to selected teams, starting with the ones asking loudest.
C. Grant seats to selected teams in waves, once policies are set.
D. Grant seats to all members on Friday for the number Elena wants.
Wave one is the platform team and Kraków, the people already using it. The integrations team waits a week for Ken's exclusions. Joyce gets a number that grows every week and a reason for each step.
That's what I'd want on my shift. Selected teams and members lets you roll out in order. Set the rules first, then hand out the keys. It's slower by days and it saves you weeks.

Ken Ito sent his message on Friday morning, polite and precise as always. Before the integrations team gets seats, I want to know which repositories hold Lumen configuration and test data. Some of it is patient adjacent. I don't want it used as context.
Nora Kim was copied. So was Joyce.
Ken doesn't want patient adjacent repositories used as Copilot context. What should Priya do?
A. Set exclusions now, grant seats today and let Ken add repos as he finds them.
B. Ask the integrations team to keep those files closed while Copilot is on.
C. Keep the integrations team off Copilot for good, with no seats at all.
D. List the sensitive repos with Ken and set exclusions before seats go out.

They find four repositories and two folders in a fifth. Ken sets the exclusions at the organization level. Nora writes one line in her evidence log: exclusions configured before access granted, with the date.

That's the one I'd sign. Content exclusions keep chosen files and repositories out of Copilot's context. On Business and Enterprise an organization owner sets them for people with org seats. Set them before the team that touches the sensitive code gets access.
Renata Vega had been at Halcyon three weeks. She was in wave one because she sat with the platform team, and on Monday she messaged Priya directly, which took courage for someone in her first month.
Sorry if this is dumb. I installed the Copilot extension in VS Code and nothing happens. No suggestions. Is it me?
Priya remembered being three weeks in and afraid to ask anything.
Renata installed the VS Code extension and gets no suggestions. What should Priya look at first?
A. Tell her it's likely a rollout delay and to wait for the next wave.
B. Check which GitHub account VS Code is signed into, work or personal.
C. Confirm her seat on the Access page, then restart the editor and retry.
D. Have her reinstall the VS Code extension from a clean download.

Renata's signed in with the personal account she made in college. Two minutes later suggestions are appearing. Priya adds "check which account you're signed into" to the top of the setup guide, and thanks Renata in the channel for finding it.

That's how I'd chart it. To use Copilot in the IDE you install the extension and sign in with the account that holds the seat. Wrong account, no Copilot. Check the simple thing first, and make it safe for new people to ask.
Anders hadn't installed it. He'd made that clear in two meetings and one very long Slack thread. People were starting to quote him, and Priya could feel the rollout bending around his doubt.

It was hard to be the one leading Anders. He had shown her where everything lived, back when she was the quietest person on the team. She still had a runbook with "ask Anders" written in the margins in her own handwriting.
Anders still hasn't installed Copilot, and people are quoting his doubt. How should Priya handle him?
A. Tell Anders that Elena's email covers contractors, him included, this week.
B. Leave Anders alone and spend the time on engineers who are already eager.
C. Ask Anders in private to try Chat on his own Terraform and judge it.
D. Ask Devin to show Anders how much faster he ships with Copilot now.

He opens one of the first modules he ever wrote and asks Copilot Chat to explain it. It gets most of it right and one thing wrong, a lifecycle rule it describes backwards. Anders is delighted to find the mistake. He's also a little annoyed at how good the rest was. Fine. It's a decent junior. A junior I have to check. That sentence does more for the rollout than any email could.

That's what I'd want on my shift. Copilot Chat can explain existing code, which speeds up learning and cuts context switching. Inviting a skeptic to test it on what he knows best turns resistance into an honest evaluation, and his review becomes the team's standard.
Nora Kim booked thirty minutes, which for Nora meant she had five questions and would ask all of them.
The SOC 2 auditors will ask who has Copilot, when they got it, and what the settings were. Can we prove that? And can we see what people typed into it?
A. Say the audit log shows seats and policy changes but no prompts, kept 180 days.
B. Set up a monthly self attestation where engineers confirm proper use.
C. Export the Access page seat list each month and hand that to the auditors.
D. Say the audit log captures everything: seats, policies, prompts and every suggestion.

Nora writes it all down. Seat grants and removals, plan and policy changes, all in the audit log for 180 days, so they'll export it every month and keep the exports for the full audit period. Prompts from editors aren't in it. Good. I'd rather know what we can't show than find out in the room.

That's the one I'd sign. The audit log records Copilot settings, policy changes, and seat changes. It doesn't include the prompts people send from their editors. Know the retention too, and plan for evidence that has to outlast it.
On Friday Elena called Priya directly, which had never happened before.
Love the progress. One idea. Let's track acceptance rates per engineer and set a target. If we're paying for it, people should be using it.
Priya thought about Devin shipping code he hadn't read. She thought about Renata, who'd be afraid of a number with her name on it.
Elena wants a target acceptance rate for each engineer. How should Priya answer?
A. Ask Elena to hold off on metrics until the end of the quarter.
B. Agree, and set a 30 percent acceptance target for every engineer.
C. Offer team adoption and defect trends instead of per person acceptance.
D. Track acceptance per person privately and talk only to those below average.

Priya won't put an acceptance target on any one engineer, and she says so. Elena pushes back for exactly one minute, then asks what outcomes Priya would report. Priya has three. Elena likes the third one best, the one about escaped defects. Fine. Show me those in a month.

That's how I'd chart it. A per person acceptance target rewards accepting suggestions, not good code. That pushes people toward overreliance, one of the main harms of generative AI. Measure outcomes and team adoption, and keep humans accountable for what they accept.

By Friday night the dashboard said fifty eight seats, every one of them on the organization plan. Wave two was scheduled. Ken's exclusions were in. Nora had a page of evidence with dates on it. It wasn't ninety yet. It was real.

She drove to Aurora on Sunday for dinner, the way she did most weeks. Her father had been a machinist for thirty one years. He could tell you the tolerance on a part by the sound it made in the lathe. He asked about work while he served the dal.
So the computer writes the code now? he said. Then what do they pay you for?
To check it, she said, and realized it was the truest thing she'd said all week. And to decide what it's allowed to touch.

He thought about that. When they put the first CNC machines in the shop, the young guys trusted them completely. The old guys didn't trust them at all. Both kinds scrapped a lot of parts. He passed her the rice. The ones who did well measured everything.

Driving home she thought about Anders calling Copilot a decent junior, and Renata finding the setup bug, and Elena saying "show me in a month." For years she had been the person who asked Anders. This week she'd been the one deciding, and he'd let her. She didn't know what to do with that yet.

At 2:14 in the morning her phone lit up on the nightstand. Tomasz, from Kraków, where it was already mid morning. We assigned the logging issue to Copilot on GitHub, like the docs say. Then we waited in our IDE for it to start working. Nothing. Where did it go?
Priya stared at the message. She realized she didn't know, either.
